scenes.narration: Microsoft is worth about three point nine six trillion dollars. That's five hundred and thirty-three dollars and sixteen cents a share at the close on November tenth, twenty twenty-six, times about seven point four billion shares. And by our math, that's sixty-six times the free cash flow it generated over the last twelve months.

Here's why that number looks so strange. Over the same twelve months, Microsoft spent about one hundred and thirty-six billion dollars on property and equipment, mostly data centers. That's thirty-nine percent of everything it sold. The cash is there. It's just being poured back into concrete, chips and cooling.
So what is this price actually betting on? What has to happen for all that spending to pay off? And what could break the story?
In the next few minutes, we open the machine, follow the cash into the data centers, run the numbers on what's priced in, and finish with the three numbers to watch when Microsoft reports next.
Quick note. This isn't financial advice. Everything here comes from Microsoft's own filings, its earnings call and our own math, dated, so you can decide for yourself.

scenes.narration: In fiscal twenty twenty-six, Microsoft brought in about three hundred and thirty-two billion dollars, up eighteen percent. And it now reports just two engines. Agents and Infra, the cloud, the A I platforms and the business software, made about two hundred and sixty-eight billion dollars, at an operating margin of about fifty-one percent. Devices and Consumer, meaning Windows, Xbox and the PCs, made about sixty-four billion dollars, and barely grew.

The engine inside the engine is Azure. It made about one hundred and two billion dollars last fiscal year. And in the September quarter alone, about thirty-three billion dollars, up forty-eight percent. That's about thirty-six percent of all of Microsoft's revenue. The Office cloud for businesses grew seventeen percent. Meanwhile, Windows sold with new PCs fell twenty-two percent.

And one customer stands out. In that quarter, Microsoft booked ten billion dollars of revenue from its arrangements with OpenAI, about eleven percent of the total. Microsoft also owns about twenty-four percent of OpenAI on an as converted basis. So OpenAI is a partner, a shareholder story, and one of Azure's biggest buyers, all at once.

Under the hood, the product lines are moving at very different speeds. the cloud Office subscriptions made about twenty-eight billion dollars in the quarter, up seventeen percent. Search and advertising grew ten percent. But the older businesses are shrinking. Windows sales to PC makers fell twenty-two percent, Xbox slipped two percent, and classic software licenses dropped three percent. So the cloud engine runs at an operating margin of almost fifty-three percent, while the consumer side is going backwards.

Let me draw the machine. Here is Agents and Infra, the big engine. Here is Devices and Consumer, the small one. Here is Azure, feeding the big engine. And this arrow is the one that matters most right now, because one customer, OpenAI, sends a tenth of the quarter's revenue through it.

scenes.narration: An engine that big throws off a lot of cash. So why is free cash flow so small?

scenes.narration: Operating cash flow over the last twelve months was about one hundred and ninety-six billion dollars. Net income was about one hundred and forty-three billion dollars. But capex took about one hundred and thirty-six billion dollars of that operating cash. What was left, the free cash flow, was about sixty billion dollars, by our math.

The latest quarter shows the trend. The C F O said free cash flow was eighteen point six billion dollars, reflecting higher capital expenditures. A year earlier it was about twenty-six billion, so that's down about twenty-seven percent. Total capex in the quarter was forty-five point two billion dollars including finance leases, or thirty-nine point four billion dollars in cash.

And there's more spending already lined up. Microsoft has three hundred and twenty-nine billion dollars of data center leases that haven't even started yet. Finance lease liabilities on the balance sheet are already seventy-one billion dollars. Much of this build-out doesn't show up as debt, but it is money Microsoft has promised to spend.

Even so, the shareholders still get paid. Over the last twelve months, buybacks and dividends came to about forty-eight billion dollars, about eighty percent of free cash flow. The share count barely moved, because buybacks mostly offset stock handed to employees.

Let me draw where twelve months of operating cash went. Here is the operating cash bar. Here is the capex bar, eating most of it. Here is what's left, the free cash flow. And here is what went back to shareholders. Almost nothing is left over after that.

scenes.narration: Three quick lenses first, all our math on the last twelve months. Price to earnings, about twenty-eight times. Free cash flow yield, about one and a half percent. Operating cash flow yield, about four point nine percent. Those last two tell very different stories, and the gap between them is the data center bill.

So for a company in a building spree, we use a proxy. We take operating cash and subtract depreciation, about about thirty-eight billion dollars a year, as a rough stand-in for the spending needed just to keep things running. That leaves about one hundred and fifty-eight billion dollars, a yield of about four percent. It's a proxy, and it assumes capex eventually falls back toward that level.

Now let's run it backwards. What growth in that cash, for ten years, makes today's price work, before slowing to three percent? With an eight percent discount rate, about five and a half percent a year. With ten percent, about ten percent. But run the same math on today's actual free cash flow, and the answer jumps to between about eighteen percent and about twenty-three percent a year.

So the real question is the capex. Here's one more lens, our rough illustration. If Microsoft keeps spending at today's pace, every dollar of capex has to add about about eighteen cents to about thirty-two cents of extra operating cash every year, within a decade, for the price to make sense.

scenes.narration: Number one, Azure keeps growing near fifty percent. The C F O guided forty-nine to fifty percent growth in constant currency for this quarter, and said customer demand continues to exceed available supply. If the new capacity lands on time, that demand turns into revenue.

Number two, the backlog converts. Microsoft's commercial backlog is six hundred and seventy-seven billion dollars, up seventy-three percent. The C F O said roughly thirty percent of it will become revenue in the next twelve months, about about two hundred billion dollars. Bookings actually fell, because last year had huge Azure deals. So the backlog has to keep refilling.

Number three, capex peaks and free cash flow recovers. For this quarter, the C F O expects capex of over fifty billion dollars, and approximately one hundred and seventy billion dollars for the calendar year. He also said Microsoft expects to remain free cash flow positive in fiscal twenty twenty-seven. The price needs a lot more than positive.

And number four, margins hold. Microsoft Cloud gross margin has already slipped to sixty-six percent, and the guide is roughly sixty-five percent, because Azure's A I work costs more to serve. Revenue for the quarter is guided at between ninety-six and ninety-seven point one billion dollars. Growth is not the problem. Profit per dollar is the thing to watch.

scenes.narration: Now the other side of the scale.

scenes.visual_objective: Chapter card: masked title reveal, gold rule draws

scenes.narration: Risk one is the build-out itself. Microsoft's own filing says these investments come in advance of fully developed revenue streams, and that the revenue may not arrive on time or at the expected levels. Overestimating demand could leave capacity sitting idle, and lead to write-downs.

Risk two is concentration. Partners like OpenAI are also big Azure customers, and Microsoft warns the benefits may not be realized or sustained. And if prices for A I services fall because of competition, margins could suffer.

And the OpenAI tie runs deeper than revenue. Microsoft owns about twenty-four percent of OpenAI on an as-converted basis. OpenAI owes it about seven billion dollars. And Microsoft has committed thirteen billion dollars of funding, with twelve billion of that already paid in. Last fiscal year, OpenAI brought in about twenty-four billion dollars of revenue, about seven percent of the total. Microsoft's own filing warns that a partnership that fails to anticipate changing circumstances may end early or be renegotiated. It doesn't put a market value on the stake, and neither will we.

Risk three is the long list in the fine print. The I R S is seeking an extra twenty-eight point nine billion dollars in tax, plus penalties and interest, for twenty oh four to twenty thirteen, which Microsoft disputes. Regulators in Europe, Britain, the U S and China are watching. And tariffs could raise costs for devices and data centers.

And the upside the price might not fully include. The C F O says Foundry revenue more than tripled. The C E O says Copilot daily users are up more than five times in a year, and Microsoft is finding ways to sell capacity that was sitting underused. None of that comes with a dollar figure, so we won't put one on it.

scenes.narration: So, what should you watch?

Here's the scorecard for the next report, expected around late January twenty twenty-seven, our estimate. One, Azure growth against the forty-nine to fifty percent guide. Two, capex, and whether free cash flow holds near eighteen point six billion dollars. Three, the backlog, and whether it broadens beyond one customer. If those hold up, the story the price is telling keeps holding up. If they crack, the capex gets much harder to defend.
That's Microsoft, November twenty twenty-six edition. We'll update it after every report, with new numbers and the same three questions. What's priced in, what has to happen, and what could go wrong.
